authors: Levant, R. F., Hall, R. J., Williams, C. M., & Hasan, N. T.
title: Gender differences in alexithymia
finding: A meta-analysis of 41 samples found that men scored slightly higher than women on alexithymia (difficulty identifying and describing feelings), but the difference was small.
strength: moderate — a meta-analysis with a consistent but small effect; self-report measures

authors: Matsumoto, D., Yoo, S. H., & Nakagawa, S.
title: Culture, emotion regulation, and adjustment
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 94(6), 925–937
finding: Across 23 countries, cultures that placed more value on social order and hierarchy tended to report more suppression of emotions; cultures valuing individual autonomy and egalitarianism reported less.
strength: moderate — large cross-cultural survey; country-level correlations, self-report
note: Some records list the 'Multinational Study of Cultural Display Rules' as a collective co-author.

authors: Ben Simon, E., & Walker, M. P.
title: Sleep loss causes social withdrawal and loneliness
finding: After a night without sleep, young adults kept an approaching person at a greater distance and felt lonelier, with brain changes linked to social avoidance; rested people who briefly watched them felt lonelier too.
strength: early — small experimental samples (18 in the main scanning study), one lab

authors: Phung, J., Penner, M., Pirlot, C., & Welch, C.
title: What I wish you knew: Insights on burnout, inertia, meltdown, and shutdown from autistic youth
finding: Interviews with eight autistic children and young people explored burnout, inertia, meltdown and shutdown as separate experiences, what they feel like, and what others do that helps or makes them worse.
strength: early — small qualitative study; builds on earlier work with autistic adults

authors: Grove, R., Hoekstra, R. A., Wierda, M., & Begeer, S.
title: Special interests and subjective wellbeing in autistic adults
finding: In a survey of autistic adults in the Netherlands Autism Register, about two-thirds reported a special interest; greater motivation for the interest was linked to higher wellbeing, while very high intensity of engagement was linked to lower wellbeing.
strength: moderate — large survey, cross-sectional and self-report
note: DOI (likely 10.1002/aur.1931) given by one secondary source only, so not used.

authors: Leedham, A., Thompson, A. R., Smith, R., & Freeth, M.
title: ‘I was exhausted trying to figure it out’: The experiences of females receiving an autism diagnosis in middle to late adulthood
finding: Interviews with eleven autistic women diagnosed at 40 or older explored how they made sense of a lifetime of feeling different and how the diagnosis changed their understanding of themselves.

authors: Mischkowski, D., Kross, E., & Bushman, B. J.
title: Flies on the wall are less aggressive: Self-distancing “in the heat of the moment” reduces aggressive thoughts, angry feelings and aggressive behavior
finding: After being provoked, people who reflected on the moment from a distanced, “fly on the wall” view felt less angry and behaved less aggressively than people who relived it from their own point of view.

title: Anger is an approach-related affect: Evidence and implications
finding: A review of evidence that anger is usually an “approach” emotion: like eagerness, it moves people toward a goal or obstacle rather than away from it.
strength: moderate — influential review; the approach view is debated (see replies in the same journal issue)

title: A meta-analysis of the psychological treatment of anger: Developing guidelines for evidence-based practice
venue: Journal of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law, 37(4), 473–488
finding: Across 96 studies and 139 treatment effects, psychological treatments for anger (such as CBT, skills training and relaxation) were generally effective, with considerable variation between treatments and studies.
strength: moderate — large meta-analysis; varied study quality and settings

authors: Laurenceau, J.-P., Barrett, L. F., & Pietromonaco, P. R.
title: Intimacy as an interpersonal process: The importance of self-disclosure, partner disclosure, and perceived partner responsiveness in interpersonal exchanges
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(5), 1238–1251
finding: Diary studies of everyday social interactions supported Reis and Shaver’s model: disclosing feelings, and feeling that the other person responded with understanding, both contributed to how intimate an interaction felt.
strength: moderate — two diary studies with students

authors: Aron, A., Melinat, E., Aron, E. N., Vallone, R. D., & Bator, R. J.
title: The experimental generation of interpersonal closeness: A procedure and some preliminary findings
finding: Pairs of strangers who spent about 45 minutes on gradually deepening self-disclosure tasks (the “36 questions”) felt closer afterwards than pairs given small-talk tasks; matching on attitudes or expecting to like each other made no significant difference.
strength: moderate — lab studies with students; creates temporary closeness, not lasting relationships
note: Link is the Greater Good in Action (UC Berkeley) page for the practice, which cites the study; the DOI (probably 10.1177/0146167297234003) was not shown directly in a search result. Must NOT be confused with aron-aron-1997 in the research index: the site links the in-text name directly.

title: Does a long-term relationship kill romantic love?
finding: Reviewing studies of short- and long-term relationships, the authors concluded that romantic love without obsession can last in long-term relationships and is linked with greater satisfaction and well-being.
strength: moderate — review and meta-analysis of mostly self-report studies

authors: Carstensen, L. L., Isaacowitz, D. M., & Charles, S. T.
title: Taking time seriously: A theory of socioemotional selectivity
finding: Proposes that perceived time left shapes social goals: when time feels open-ended people seek new information and contacts; when it feels limited they focus on fewer, emotionally meaningful relationships.
strength: strong — widely supported theory, though causal tests are harder

authors: Kardas, M., Kumar, A., & Epley, N.
title: Overly shallow?: Miscalibrated expectations create a barrier to deeper conversation
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 122(3), 367–398
finding: People expected deep conversations with strangers to be more awkward and less enjoyable than they turned out to be; deeper talks created more connection and happiness than predicted.
note: Authors, title, year, journal, volume and pages confirmed; no DOI or publisher page appeared in search results, so no link. The site names it in text without a link.

title: The problem of meaning in primitive languages
venue: Supplement I in C. K. Ogden & I. A. Richards, The Meaning of Meaning. Kegan Paul / Harcourt, Brace
finding: Coined “phatic communion”: everyday talk whose main purpose is social bonding rather than passing on information.
strength: foundational idea in linguistics and anthropology, not an empirical study
note: The essay and the coinage are confirmed, but page numbers differ by edition and no stable publisher link was found. Named in text without a link.

authors: Reis, H. T., Clark, M. S., & Holmes, J. G.
title: Perceived partner responsiveness as an organizing construct in the study of intimacy and closeness
venue: In D. J. Mashek & A. Aron (Eds.), Handbook of Closeness and Intimacy (pp. 201–225). Lawrence Erlbaum
finding: Argues that feeling understood, valued and cared for by a partner (perceived responsiveness) is central to intimacy and closeness.
note: Chapter and pages confirmed via a review and later citations; no stable link to the chapter itself. Named in text without a link (wrapped in .no-research).
